strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and under-studied failure mode in GUI agents: binary toggle control, especially false positives when the desired state already matches the current state. This is a practically important problem for mobile agents and safety-sensitive UI automation.

The proposed state-control benchmark is large, with 81,836 positive/negative instruction samples derived from multiple public GUI datasets, and the paper evaluates a broad set of proprietary and open-source agents. The diagnostic metrics separate action type, coordinate grounding, false negatives, and false positives, which gives useful insight beyond a single aggregate score.

StaR is simple but effective: training agents to explicitly perceive current state, infer desired state, and decide whether to click yields large gains on the benchmark, e.g. O-AMR improves from 43.95 to 79.72 for OS-Atlas-7B and from 47.45 to 77.86 for UI-TARS-7B.

The paper includes several useful comparisons, including ordinary prompting, StaR-style prompting, ground-truth state prompting, component ablations, static agentic benchmarks, and a small dynamic Android evaluation. These results support the claim that training is more effective than merely adding a state-aware prompt.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited. StaR is essentially supervised fine-tuning with templated reasoning traces for a three-step state-checking procedure. The reasoning structure is sensible, but technically straightforward, and the paper sometimes presents this as a more substantial reasoning method than the evidence warrants.

The benchmark quality is a material concern. Labels are generated by proprietary MLLM annotators and filtered by agreement, but only 200 samples are manually verified, with 91% state accuracy and 92.5% functionality accuracy. For a benchmark intended to train and evaluate fine-grained toggle behavior, an estimated 8-9% label error rate is nontrivial.

The benchmark is highly imbalanced by source: Table 3 shows AITW accounts for 68,380/73,652 train samples and 7,558/8,184 test samples. This weakens claims of broad GUI diversity despite listing several datasets, since most sources contribute very few test examples.

The evaluation is partly in-domain and may overstate generalization. StaR is trained on the same constructed benchmark distribution used for the main test, and the public agentic benchmarks used for generalization are also included in training via their training splits. The reported general improvements therefore do not cleanly isolate transfer to unseen task families or annotation styles.

The dynamic evaluation is too small to strongly support real-world applicability: it has only 20 tasks, many are simple WiFi/Bluetooth/alarm/Chrome toggles, and success-rate differences correspond to small counts. This is useful as a sanity check but not enough for the broad real-world claims made in the text.

The paper does not sufficiently analyze whether gains come from state-aware reasoning versus ordinary additional supervised training on toggle examples. A stronger control would fine-tune on the same toggle data without StaR-formatted reasoning, or with non-state templated rationales, across all agents.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The abstract contains an empty 'Code and benchmark:' field, and many key details depend on proprietary annotators and generated reasoning traces. Without released data, prompts, and annotation outputs, reproducing both the benchmark and the main training results would be difficult.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and practically relevant failure mode for GUI agents: unnecessary or omitted clicks on binary toggles when the current state must be compared with the desired state.

The state-control benchmark is large in scale and the evaluation covers several proprietary and open-source GUI/multimodal agents, giving useful empirical evidence that current agents often over-toggle, especially on negative cases where the goal is already satisfied.
StaR training produces large gains on the proposed benchmark, especially reducing false-positive toggling: e.g., OS-Atlas-7B O-AMR improves from 43.95 to 79.72 and N-AMR from 35.80 to 96.48.
The paper includes several helpful baselines beyond simple prompting, ablations over perceiving/analyzing/deciding components, and a small dynamic AndroidWorld-style evaluation.
weaknesses: The core method is technically modest: it is supervised fine-tuning on automatically generated state-aware rationales for a narrowly defined toggle task. The paper frames this as a reasoning method, but the contribution is closer to data construction plus rationale-style fine-tuning, with limited algorithmic novelty.

Benchmark reliability is a major concern. Toggle identification, state, and functionality labels are generated by proprietary MLLMs, with only 200 final samples manually verified; the reported 91% state accuracy implies substantial label noise for a benchmark whose main claim depends precisely on state correctness. The independence assumption behind the theoretical agreement estimate is also weak for two similar MLLM annotators.

The dataset is heavily imbalanced by source: the test split has 7,558/8,184 samples from AITW and only tiny counts from several other datasets. This weakens claims about diverse GUI coverage and generalization.

There is risk of circularity and leakage. Qwen-2-VL-72B is both part of the annotation pipeline and an evaluated baseline, and the training also uses AndroidControl/AITZ/GUI-Odyssey training splits that the paper says are already part of the original training sets of all agents. The paper does not clearly rule out near-duplicate screens, apps, or instructions between training and testing.

The general agentic benchmark improvements are confounded. StaR-trained models receive additional training on the agentic benchmark training splits, so improvements cannot be attributed cleanly to the StaR reasoning structure without a control that uses the same data and compute but ordinary rationales or no StaR-style refinement.

The dynamic evaluation is too small to support the strong real-world applicability claims: only 20 tasks are used, partial success scoring is allowed, and no confidence intervals or repeated-run variance are reported. Gains such as 7/20 to 8/20 for UI-TARS are not compelling evidence of robustness.

Several baselines are conceptually questionable. The paper calls ground-truth toggle-state prompting a theoretical upper bound for training-free multi-agent collaboration, yet it performs below StaR training in many cases, suggesting either the baseline is poorly instantiated or the interpretation is invalid.

The main metric, exact action match rate, is tied to generated bounding-box labels and may not reflect functional success in actual GUIs. Positive examples require matching a coordinate, while negative examples require only COMPLETED, so the balanced synthetic setup can obscure different error costs.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the abstract has an empty 'Code and benchmark:' field, and key details about data release, filtering, deduplication, annotation prompts’ outputs, and training data mixtures are insufficient for independent replication.

Presentation is often overclaiming. Phrases such as 'intrinsic reasoning capability' and 'real-world applicability' are stronger than the evidence supports, given the supervised fine-tuning setup, noisy automatic labels, and limited dynamic evaluation.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and important failure mode for multimodal GUI agents: toggles require state perception, desired-state inference, and a decision to act or stop. The constructed state-control benchmark is well motivated and exposes a clear false-positive toggling bias across many current agents, including proprietary and open-source systems.

The proposed StaR training recipe is simple but effective. Results on the state-control benchmark are strong, with O-AMR improving by 14.9 to 35.8 points across four trained agents, mainly through large gains on negative samples and false-positive reduction.

The experimental section is broader than a single-model demonstration: it covers several GUI agents, compares prompting, StaR-style prompting, and ground-truth-state prompting baselines, and includes component ablations showing that perceiving/analyzing/deciding together work best.

The paper makes a plausible case that the method does not merely overfit to the custom benchmark: agentic benchmark results are mostly preserved or improved, and the dynamic AndroidWorld-style evaluation, although small, supports the practical relevance of the failure mode.

The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful prompt templates, implementation details, metrics, data-source breakdowns, and training hyperparameters, making the core approach reasonably reproducible if the benchmark/code are released as promised.
weaknesses: The main technical contribution is closer to supervised fine-tuning on structured reasoning traces than a fundamentally new reasoning method. The StaR formulation is intuitive and useful, but the novelty is moderate because the method is essentially a task-specific chain-of-thought template plus curated toggle data.

Benchmark reliability is a meaningful concern. Toggle identity, state, and functionality are annotated by MLLM agreement, and the final manual audit covers only 200 samples with about 91% state accuracy. Correlated annotator errors are likely, so the theoretical independence-based estimate of annotation quality is not very convincing.

The state-control benchmark is heavily dominated by AITW-derived samples, with very few examples from several listed sources. The paper does not sufficiently analyze diversity, app-level/screenshot-level leakage, or whether near-duplicate screens/functions appear across train and test splits, which matters for a fine-tuned method.

The benchmark construction creates paired positive/negative instructions from the same annotated toggle. This is useful diagnostically, but it can make the task distribution artificial: every negative example has a deterministic stop label and every positive example clicks the target box, which may not fully reflect open-ended GUI use.

Some claims about reasoning are stronger than the evidence. Improvements may partly come from better grounding and memorization of toggle visual patterns after fine-tuning, not necessarily from learning a general state-aware reasoning process. The ablations help but do not fully disentangle data effects from reasoning-format effects.

The dynamic evaluation is too small for strong real-world claims: only 20 tasks are used, with no confidence intervals, repeated-run variance, or broader app/device coverage. It is encouraging but should be framed as preliminary evidence.

General agentic benchmark comparisons are somewhat difficult to interpret because the agents are further trained on benchmark training splits that overlap with common pretraining/fine-tuning sources, and the evaluation is mostly static action matching rather than end-to-end execution. Some reported improvements may reflect formatting/training alignment rather than general task competence.

Presentation has several polish issues, including typos, awkward phrasing, and table extraction/rendering oddities such as compact success-rate notation in Table 2. These do not undermine the core contribution but reduce clarity.
